lines: Every version of this seen so far keeps the one true copy right next to the machine doing the work.
That was never forced on anyone. It was simply the choice made, every time, up to now.
What actually changes once something decides to do the opposite, on purpose, for once?
One earlier way keeps everything sitting in memory, right there on the same machine.
A different earlier way keeps it on that same machine's own disk instead, just a bit slower.
Either way, so far, the true copy has never left that one machine at all.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Suppose that one true copy moves off the machine entirely, out onto storage somewhere else.
What happens, then, to the cost of taking a fresh picture of everything right now?
answer: Barely anything changes about that cost at all, and here's why.
The copy a fresh picture would need to save was already sitting out there, saved already.
So there's almost nothing left to actually move. Just a little bookkeeping about what already exists.

lines: The new way of holding things is built the same way an older local one was, just pointed elsewhere.
Its own files live out on storage somewhere else entirely, not on the one machine doing the work.
What's left on that machine becomes a cache for speed, never the one true copy anymore.
Because the true copy already sits durably out where a fresh picture would save it anyway,
taking that picture collapses down into barely more than noting what already exists out there.
A full save becomes close to free, once nothing heavy actually has to move anymore.
Coming back after a failure gets measurably faster, following straight from that same cause.
Growing bigger gets measurably faster too, for exactly the same underlying reason.
Shrinking down afterward speeds up right along with it, all three tracing back to one single change.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
Every single touch of what's being held can now cross over a real distance, out and back.
If every one of those touches still just sat there and waited its turn, what would that do?
answer: Everything slows to a crawl, unless waiting stops being required at all.
Blocking on each and every one of those round trips would stall absolutely everything behind it.
So the whole way of asking for something has to change, not just where it's kept.

lines: One older way of asking waits right there until the answer comes all the way back.
A newer way hands back something else instead, right away, without waiting at all.
That lets one request's own round trip overlap cleanly with a completely different one's.
Here's the one guarantee that makes all of that genuinely safe to do.
Anything touching the exact same thing twice still finishes in the exact order it was asked for, always.
Anything touching two different things entirely is free to finish in whatever order it happens to land in.
Running with nothing kept close by at all does measurably hurt how much gets through, and that's real.
But keeping even a modest amount close by earns almost all of that back again.
It ends up ahead of the older, fully local way it's replacing, even with just a little kept close.
Every single number in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy model.
The cost of a fresh picture that stayed flat, no matter how much there was to begin with.
Touching the same thing twice that stayed ordered, while touching two different things freely overlapped.
So: the one true copy moved off the machine, entirely on purpose, for once.
Taking a fresh picture paid that move straight back, by turning into something close to free.
Waiting less hides the extra distance, without ever breaking what order actually mattered. A cache left cold is the real price.
